cells.A1: SaveMore: LTV/CAC model (the main case, 24 Oct 2026)
cells.A2: What one saver won is worth, with every assumption visible: the investor plan's own model, rebuilt here cell by cell.
cells.A3: LTV/CAC = what a saver brings in over 5 or 8 years, less the cost of serving them, divided by what it costs to win them. On 24 Oct the founders fixed every input (market figures, a daily-savings app, or our judgement). Two are still uncertain and the Monte Carlo draws them (we ran the model 1,000 times, picking retention, 30%–40% still saving at 12 months, and the debt fund's fee, 0.10%–0.35%, at random within their ranges). The values on Inputs are the MAIN CASE, the median draw.
cells.A6: Cross-selling alone (loans and cards): ₹143 per saver in 5 years, ₹173 in 8. That is 0.29× and 0.35× of the ₹495 it costs to win a saver, and less than the ₹190 / ₹225 it costs to serve them, so on its own it never pays back (−0.10× after serving). Insurance, recharge, bills, FD and NPS are not counted.
cells.A7: With fund fees, 0.75× in 5 years and 1.32× in 8 (net of serving); it pays back in month 75. At market numbers this is a fund-fee business; loans are a small add-on.
cells.A8: Assumes debits cost us ₹0 and a 0.75% equity fund fee, both still to be confirmed in writing (₹2 a weekly debit would cut a saver to about 0.39×, a 0.5% fee to about 0.49×). The cost to win is ₹450 at scale (the founders' figure; they call it 'fairly sorted') plus the 10% contingency = ₹495; the seed budgets ₹600 while the brand is new, and measures it. At ₹600 (₹660 with the contingency) a saver is about 0.56× / 0.99×.
cells.A9: Still uncertain, mostly how long savers keep saving: 8 in 10 draws land between 0.60× and 0.93× at 5 years, and between 1.00× and 1.76× at 8. 0.3% of the 1,000 draws reach 1× in 5 years and 90% by 8, holding everything else at the main case.
cells.A10: What it takes for 1× in 5 years, one lever alone: ₹130 a day on average (₹100 is our product's floor), or 40.5% still saving at 12 months. No single loan lever gets there (applications from 35% of users a year give 0.92×). 1× needs ₹115 a day, 36% still saving, 22% applying and 22% approved together (still not EBITDA-positive by month 96, $8.1M+). 2× needs ₹161 a day, 41% still saving, 29% applying and 26% approved together (EBITDA positive from month 68, $5.1M). 3× needs ₹194 a day, 44% still saving, 34% applying and 29% approved together (EBITDA positive from month 55, $4.0M).
cells.A11: The company (20,000 online savers a month from month 30): EBITDA (operating profit before interest, tax and depreciation) is not positive by month 96 in any of the 1,000 draws; money needed $9.3M+ at the median (still losing money at month 96, so at least this). Each saver costs more than it earns back within 5 years, so growing faster deepens the loss.

cells.A29: Revenue = what we are paid: our trail on the fund balance (the fund fee), lenders' payouts and referral fees on loans, and card fees (3% of savers still saving at month 7 take one). Insurance (a fixed broker fee, to be agreed) is not counted; recharge, bills, FD and NPS are not in the launch app; nor loans against savings (10% of applications). The app never holds the money: funds are bought in the saver's own name, and a saver who stops withdraws everything, so fund fees stop.
cells.A30: Serving = support ₹5 a month per saver still saving, tech ₹4 a month for every KYC'd user reached, and payments (₹0 a debit), plus the plan's 10% contingency. LTV = revenue less serving over 5 years, undiscounted (8 years alongside). Pays back = the first month cumulative revenue less serving reaches the cost to win.
cells.A31: A saver who joins in the business's month 1. Loan take-up and approvals do not rise with the business's years (today's market rates); lenders' caution in a user's first 6 months is kept.
cells.A32: Loans: offers reach the saver and the KYC'd users who came with them (about 2.5 a saver); those who never save fade within about 3 months, so the reach of 1.06 per online saver won is a value weight (only the tech cost scales with it); doorstep 1.
cells.A33: Not in this view: the team, office and brand (company costs, in our business-plan model), the 2-month wait for fees to arrive, tax.
cells.A35: THE FOUR FACTS THAT DECIDE IT, ALL CHEAP TO GET
cells.A36: 1. The AVERAGE daily amount at a daily-savings app (₹100 is our floor; a daily-savings app's own minimums are lower). 2. The exact 12-month retention at a daily-savings app. 3. The ₹0 debit cost in writing (BSE and the fund houses; one hybrid fund at ₹100 a day). 4. The fee on the fund the ₹100 goes into, in writing (0.64% blended or better: 80% equity at 0.75% and 20% debt at about 0.22%).
cells.A39: The sheet's formulas were replayed by a formula interpreter and match the plan's model at the main case and at 5 Monte Carlo draws: LTV/CAC to 6 decimals, the payback month exactly, every monthly line to 1 part in 100 million.
cells.A40: The Monte Carlo is the LTV/CAC Monte Carlo's 1,000 draws: the cost to win and every fixed input held, 2 inputs drawn; each draw's LTV/CAC sits next to that draw's company EBITDA month, and the median draw is the main case.
